The group excels at converting complex technical criteria into clear, user-focused software concepts, and is seeking teammates skilled in coding, visual design, media production, or domain research.
summary:
OrthoSpace is a project we developed to help astronauts monitor their health during space missions, especially when returning to gravity after spending a long time in space.

The idea is to create a system that tracks blood pressure, heart rate, symptoms and hydration levels to help astronauts notice unusual changes in their bodies. It uses personal health baselines and a simple green, yellow and red alert system to show when everything looks normal, when something needs to be checked, or when medical attention is needed.

We chose this challenge because spending months in microgravity affects the body, making it harder for astronauts to maintain normal blood pressure when they return to gravity. This can lead to dizziness or even fainting, which could put astronauts at risk during important mission activities. Our goal is to make monitoring easier, help astronauts recognize potential problems earlier and give the medical team useful information to make decisions.
details:
OrthoSpace is a system we designed to help astronauts keep track of their health while living in space and when returning to a planet like Earth or Mars.

When astronauts spend months in space, their bodies get used to living without normal gravity. Their body fluids shift, and their cardiovascular system, which controls blood circulation and blood pressure, adapts to this environment. When they return to gravity, their bodies may struggle to adjust. This can cause dizziness, blurred vision or even fainting.

Our idea is to create an application that monitors important health information, including blood pressure, heart rate, symptoms, hydration and recent physical activity. It compares this information with the astronaut's usual readings and displays one of three colours. Green means everything looks normal, yellow means something should be checked again, and red means the astronaut should stop the test and contact the medical team.

We also included two different ways to check the astronaut's condition. One is designed for use during spaceflight, using special thigh cuffs that are released to observe changes in blood pressure. The other is performed after landing, where the astronaut stands up while their blood pressure and heart rate are monitored.

OrthoSpace could make health monitoring easier and help astronauts notice unusual changes before they become more serious. This is especially important for future Mars missions, where astronauts may not have immediate access to medical support from Earth.

What makes our idea different is that it brings several health measurements together instead of relying on just one. It also takes into account that astronauts need different testing methods depending on whether they are in space or have returned to gravity.

While developing the concept, we considered astronaut safety, the effects of microgravity, equipment availability, measurement accuracy and the limited medical support available during deep space missions. We also made sure that the application would not diagnose or treat astronauts. It only provides information to support medical decisions, which remain the responsibility of the flight surgeon.

We used scientific research from NASA, the Canadian Space Agency and medical studies to guide our design. We also used digital design and presentation tools to develop and explain the concept. The blood pressure monitors, heart rate monitors and thigh cuffs are proposed equipment for a future version. Our current project is a concept, and it still needs to be tested and medically validated before it could be used on an actual space mission.
